summary: Looks back at the worm infestation of the Internet that began the evening of 2 November 1988. It provides information about the event and does not specify any standard.

eli5.summary: A bad program spread from computer to computer and made many of them very sick. This is the story of what happened.

subtitle: A comprehensive look at the 1988 Internet worm incident and its aftermath

tldr.problem: On November 2, 1988, a self-replicating program—the Internet worm—infected VAX computers and Sun-3 workstations running Berkeley UNIX, exploiting known security vulnerabilities in sendmail and fingerd and spreading rapidly across the network.
tldr.mechanism: The worm used sendmail's debug command to install itself remotely, caused buffer overflows in fingerd to gain code execution, exploited trusted host features, and guessed weak passwords to propagate to new machines. Teams at Berkeley and MIT decompiled the worm, identified its attack methods, and coordinated the distribution of patches to close the vulnerabilities.
tldr.outcome: The worm was eliminated from most systems within 48–72 hours through coordinated patch deployment. It catalyzed widespread adoption of ethical standards by the IAB, NSF, MIT, and CPSR, and prompted development of computer security legislation, though also revealed tensions between open scientific collaboration and network security.

facts.value: VAX and SUN-3 workstations running Berkeley UNIX 4.2 and 4.3

facts.value: sendmail debug command, fingerd buffer overflow, trusted hosts (rexec, rsh)

today: The Morris worm of 1988 remains a pivotal moment in Internet history, representing the first large-scale incident of its kind. It catalyzed the establishment of computer ethics standards and prompted legal frameworks around computer crime, though many questions about balancing openness and security remain unresolved today.

sections.title: The Worm Infestation of November 1988
sections.content:
On the evening of November 2, 1988, a self-replicating program escaped into the Internet, infecting VAX computers and SUN-3 workstations running Berkeley UNIX (versions 4.2 and 4.3). The program, now known as the Morris worm, exploited known but unpatched security flaws to propagate rapidly across network-connected systems. Within hours, infected sites experienced severe performance degradation and system instability. System administrators scrambled to isolate machines, patch vulnerabilities, and prevent reinfection as the worm spread unchecked across the United States.

This RFC provides a historical account of the worm incident, including its infection methods, the coordinated response that stopped it, and the broader societal questions it raised about ethics, security, law, and the Internet's future.
sections.eli5: A computer program learned to copy itself and spread to other machines, making them sick. Experts worked day and night to understand it and teach everyone how to stop it.

sections.title: How the Worm Attacked and Spread
sections.content:
The worm specifically targeted Berkeley UNIX systems and used multiple attack vectors. It exploited a non-standard debug command in sendmail, a program that handles email delivery, to remotely install itself on connected hosts. On VAX machines running 4.3BSD, it caused a buffer overflow in fingerd, a utility that provides user information, by sending far more data than the program's buffer could hold. This overflow allowed the worm to execute arbitrary code and gain system access. The worm also abused trusted host features (rexec, rsh) that allowed password-free access between systems, compromised accounts, and guessed weak passwords from a dictionary of 432 personalized words and the standard UNIX dictionary.

Once installed, the worm entered a password-cracking phase, attempting common passwords derived from user information in the /etc/passwd file. It was deliberately designed to hide its presence, leaving minimal evidence in system logs or temporary files.
sections.eli5: The worm had several sneaky ways to get in: it tricked email programs into running its code, overflowed programs by sending too much data, guessed easy passwords, and pretended to be trusted machines.

sections.title: The Community Response and Cure
sections.content:
Teams of computer scientists and students at Berkeley and MIT worked feverishly to understand the worm. They isolated infected systems to extract binary copies, then decompiled the code back to source form to study its mechanisms. The two teams communicated extensively, comparing findings and developing defenses. Through the 'old boy network'—established relationships and informal trust among senior researchers—they rapidly shared patches via email and phone calls, coordinating a community-wide response.

System administrators were instructed to patch sendmail, disable or fix fingerd, close trusted-host vulnerabilities, and implement new passwords. Within 48 to 72 hours, most infected systems had been cleaned and patched. Academic sites were especially effective in the response, while government and commercial organizations took longer to recognize and respond to the threat.
sections.eli5: The smartest computer experts met up and figured out the worm's tricks. They called all their friends to spread the word about how to fix it, and everyone patched their computers before the worm could spread more.

sections.title: Immediate Impact and Ethical Debates
sections.content:
The worm incident shook the Internet community and ignited fierce debate. Some argued it was an accident, that the worm 'escaped' from a researcher's experimental environment. Others believed it was a deliberate act to expose negligence in security practices. Some media voices portrayed the worm's author as a genius or hero for highlighting flaws that the community had known about but failed to fix. The Internet Activities Board (IAB), National Science Foundation (NSF), MIT, and Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility (CPSR) quickly issued formal ethics statements establishing that any intentional or negligent disruption of network services, unauthorized access, or destruction of data was unethical and unacceptable.

The incident revealed both the strength and vulnerability of the open research community: rapid communication and trust enabled a quick cure, but the same openness that made the Internet valuable for collaboration also made it fragile against malicious actors.
sections.eli5: People had big arguments about whether this was an accident or on purpose, and whether it was good or bad. Everyone agreed it was wrong to mess with other people's computers, but they also didn't want to shut down the Internet.

sections.title: Long-Term Lessons and Unanswered Questions
sections.content:
The incident prompted discussions across multiple domains. Legal consequences remained pending, with the accused identified but the case bringing few precedents. Several states and the federal level (HR-6061, the Computer Virus Eradication Act of 1988) began developing legislation to address computer crime. From a technical standpoint, defenses needed to be at the host level, not network-wide, since the network infrastructure itself had performed correctly—the flaws were in application software.

The documentation review in the RFC examined four major analyses of the incident, capturing chronology, technical details, and systemic lessons. Open questions remained: How should the research community balance absolute openness with security? Should known vulnerabilities be published to force fixes, or concealed? How can we prevent future incidents without creating a surveillance state or destroying the scientific ethos of the Internet?
sections.eli5: The worm taught people that security holes need to be fixed, that you can't just hope bad things won't happen, and that there are hard choices between keeping the Internet open and keeping it safe.
